Lecture 14 · OverviewFocus and Must Know

Lecturer: Prof Andrew Flatau, BDS (Hons 1), BA (Hons 1), PhD, FPFA, FICD — Centre for Rural Dentistry & Oral Health.

Focus: Learning objective focus: the cranial nerves; the infratemporal fossa, especially the pterygomandibular space; the tissues in the path of LA needles; and the significance of anatomical variation.

Must know

  • Spinal trigeminal subnuclei, rostral → caudal: oralis, interpolaris, caudalis.
  • Mylohyoid nerve = the most documented accessory supply to mandibular teeth (up to 60%).
  • The sphenomandibular ligament can shield the mylohyoid nerve from an IAN block.
  • Pterygomandibular space: below lateral pterygoid, between ramus and interpterygoid fascia.
  • IAN block: coronoid notch level, from the contralateral premolars, about 25 mm deep.
  • Needle too far posterior → parotid gland → temporary facial nerve palsy.
  • Children: foramen lower and further back; 10 or 20 mm needles.

Key to markers

  • (textbook) — fact from standard anatomy texts, not on the slides.
  • Check (red box) — the slide differs from standard texts.
  • Where a Check note applies, answer exam questions from the lecture unless told otherwise.
  • Ochre box — exam point or clinical point.

Lecture 14 · Part 1 · pp. 3–4Trigeminal Sensory Pathway

The V brainstem sensory nuclear complex (VBSNC) has two parts:

  1. Main (principal, pontine) sensory nucleus
  2. Spinal tract nucleus, with three subnuclei from rostral to caudal: oralis (Vo), interpolaris (Vi), caudalis (Vc)

Two other trigeminal nuclei:

  • Mesencephalic nucleus
  • Motor nucleus. Its fibres leave in the motor root and join V3 in the foramen ovale. They supply the muscles of the 1st arch.

Nociceptive neurons in the VBSNC project to the thalamus and to other higher CNS centres.

NucleusFunction (textbook)
MesencephalicProprioception from muscles of mastication and periodontal ligament
Principal sensoryFine (discriminative) touch
Spinal (especially caudalis)Pain and temperature
  • Sölder lines: the face is mapped in an "onion-skin" pattern. Areas around the mouth and nose map to the rostral part of the spinal nucleus; outer areas of the face map more caudally.

Lecture 14 · Part 2 · pp. 5–6Middle Cranial Fossa Dissection

Structures shown
Trigeminal ganglion, V2, V3Sensory and motor roots Genu of VIIGreater petrosal nerve Middle meningeal arteryAuditory tube Tensor tympaniAnterior ligament of malleus TMJ articular disc
  • Chorda tympani runs in the petrotympanic fissure.
  • Some fibres of the lateral pterygoid attach to the disc–capsule complex of the TMJ.

Lecture 14 · Part 3 · pp. 7–8Landmarks

  • Coronoid notch: the concavity on the anterior border of the ramus. It marks the height of the IAN block injection.
  • Temporalis tendon: inserts on the coronoid process and anterior border of the ramus. Its deep tendon forms the lateral boundary of the IAN block needle path.
  • Deep masseter and temporomasseteric fibres insert into the temporalis tendon.

Lecture 14 · Part 4 · p. 9Branches of V3

PartBranches (textbook organisation)
Main trunkMeningeal branch; nerve to medial pterygoid
Anterior division (mainly motor)Masseteric, deep temporal, nerve to lateral pterygoid, buccal (sensory only)
Posterior division (mainly sensory)Auriculotemporal, lingual, inferior alveolar (gives the mylohyoid nerve, dental branches, mental and incisive nerves)

Lecture 14 · Part 5 · pp. 10–15, 21Accessory Innervation of Mandibular Teeth

A major anatomical reason an IAN block fails.

Sources of accessory nerve supply

  1. High branches of V3 in the infratemporal fossa. They pass in front of the IAN and mandibular foramen, enter foramina on the ramus, and supply M2 and M3.
  2. Branches of V3 or the IAN that enter retromolar foramina and supply the molars.
  3. Mylohyoid nerve: the most documented source.
  4. Long buccal nerve branches that enter retromolar foramina and supply the molars.
  5. Lingual nerve collateral branches to the lingual gingiva around M3 and the retromolar pad. These may enter accessory foramina.
  6. Incisive nerve: branches extensively and can supply incisors on the opposite side.

Mylohyoid nerve

  • Traditional view: a motor nerve to mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric.
  • It also gives accessory sensory supply to:
    • Mandibular teeth from incisors to M1, in up to 60% of people
    • Submental skin
  • Routes into the mandible:
    • Retromental foramina in the PM2 region
    • Accessory foramina in the anterior mandible (found in 50% of 26 cadavers, Madeira 1978)
  • Origin: from the IAN about 14 mm above the mandibular foramen (range 5–23 mm). It occasionally arises from the main V3 trunk.
  • In about 30% of people, the mylohyoid groove is covered by bone or periosteum, giving a canal-like appearance.
  • Its fibre diameters cover both the sensory and the motor range, so it may be a mixed nerve. This is not proven.
Why the IAN block misses it: the sphenomandibular ligament and pterygomandibular fascia can shield the mylohyoid nerve from the anaesthetic.

Pulpal pain fibres

FibreMyelinDiameterSpeedPain
AδMyelinated2–10 µm (slide)5–30 m/sSharp pain; responds to pulp sensibility tests
CUnmyelinated0.5–1 µm<2 m/sSlow, dull pain; linked to pathology
Check: most physiology and endodontic textbooks give Aδ diameter as about 1–5 µm, not 2–10 µm.

Lecture 14 · Part 6 · pp. 16–17Mandibular Canal Variations

  • The course of the mandibular canal varies, and bifid canals occur.
  • Naitoh et al. (2009) used CBCT and found 114 bifid canals in 79 of 122 patients. Their classification:
TypeNameDescription
IRetromolar canalReaches a foramen in the retromolar region
IIDental canalReaches the apices of M2 and M3
IIIForward canalRuns forward, with or without rejoining the main canal
IVBuccolingual canalArises from the buccal or lingual wall of the main canal
  • The IAN can form a neurovascular plexus rather than a single nerve.

Lecture 14 · Part 7 · pp. 18–20IAN and Lingual Nerve Variations

Variants

  • Communication between the lingual nerve and the IAN
  • Communication between the mylohyoid and lingual nerves, especially near M3
  • Accessory roots of the IAN (the "lesser IAN of Sapolini") from the trigeminal ganglion
  • A single shared trunk for the IAN and lingual nerve
  • The inferior alveolar artery passing through the IAN

Dissection studies

  • Kim (2004): lingual nerve twigs to the retromolar area in 81.2% of 32 hemifaces.
  • Erdogmus (2008): in 42 hemifaces, the lingual nerve communicated with:
Communicated withFrequency
IAN47.6% (mostly above the mandibular notch)
Auriculotemporal nerve14.3%
Mylohyoid nerve11.9%
Nerve to medial pterygoid4.8%

Where the lingual nerve and IAN split (Kim 2004)

TypeLevel of split
Type 1Above the mandibular notch
Type 2Upper half between the notch and the lingula
Type 3Lower half between the notch and the lingula
Type 4Plexus (network) pattern

Lecture 14 · Part 8 · pp. 22–24Buccal Nerve

  • Also called the long buccal or buccinator nerve.
  • It is closely related to the temporalis tendon and its sheath, the temporo-buccinator band (Sloman 1939).

Course and supply (textbook)

  • It is sensory only and passes between the two heads of the lateral pterygoid.
  • It crosses the anterior border of the ramus.
  • It supplies the buccal mucosa, the buccal gingiva of the mandibular molars, and the skin of the cheek.
  • It pierces buccinator but does not supply it; buccinator is supplied by VII.
Clinical: it is not anaesthetised by an IAN block, so a separate long buccal injection is needed. (textbook)

Lecture 14 · Part 9 · pp. 25–27Posterior Superior Alveolar (PSA) Nerve

  • The PSA neurovascular bundle is held against the maxillary tuberosity by a flap of fibrous tissue, the PSA fascial sling.

Related structures

  • Facial vein
  • Deep facial vein, which connects the facial vein to the pterygoid plexus
  • Gingival artery
  • Gingival branches of the PSA nerve, which emerge from the front edge of the sling
Clinical: because the pterygoid plexus is close, a PSA block carries a risk of haematoma. (textbook)

Lecture 14 · Part 10 · pp. 28–29Maxillary Nerve Variations

  • The PSA nerve may have 1–3 branches.
  • Maxillary molars can also be supplied by palatine nerves.
  • The middle superior alveolar (MSA) nerve runs in the lateral wall of the maxillary sinus to the premolars. It is often absent or forms part of a plexus.
  • The anterior superior alveolar (ASA) nerve arises from the infraorbital nerve at a variable distance from the infraorbital foramen. It is the main contributor to the superior dental plexus.
  • The nerve supply of the maxillary M1, especially the mesiobuccal root, is debated. Classical teaching says the MSA supplies it.

Lecture 14 · Part 11 · p. 30Sphenomandibular Ligament (SML)

  • It is a thickening of the interpterygoid fascia.
  • The interpterygoid fascia runs down from the skull base, between the pterygoid muscles, to the lingula. Posteriorly it reaches the mandibular border and the stylomandibular membrane.
  • The SML runs from the spine of the sphenoid and the petrotympanic fissure to the lingula.
  • It varies from a thin band to a broad ligament.
Link to Lecture 15: the SML is a remnant of Meckel's cartilage (1st arch). See Arch derivatives.

Lecture 14 · Part 12 · pp. 32–44Pterygomandibular Space and the IAN Block

Definition (Dempster): the region below the lateral pterygoid, between the medial surface of the ramus and the interpterygoid fascia.

Boundaries (textbook)

SideBoundary
LateralRamus
MedialMedial pterygoid
SuperiorLateral pterygoid
AnteriorPterygomandibular raphe
PosteriorParotid gland

Contents

  • IAN, inferior alveolar artery and veins
  • Lingual nerve
  • SML
  • Loose fat

The interpterygoid fascia can separate the lingual nerve from the IAN. The veins usually lie behind the artery, but the reverse is also found.

Buccal pad vs buccal fat pad

  • The buccal pad is the mucosal bulge. Its apex is the injection landmark.
  • The buccal fat pad is the deeper fat mass.
Identify on a transverse section above the lingula
IAN, IAA, IAVsLingual nerveMasseterMedial pterygoid BuccinatorSuperior constrictorPterygomandibular raphe and fold Stylomandibular membraneTemporopterygoid fasciaInterpterygoid fascia SMLBuccal pad and buccal fat padTemporalis tendon Pterygotemporal depressionParotid gland with facial nerve Retromandibular veinExternal carotid arteryStyloid process

IAN block needle path

  • Enters through the injection triangle.
  • Runs between the deep temporalis tendon and the medial pterygoid.
  • Stays lateral to the pterygomandibular raphe and fold. The fold is superficial to the raphe.
  • Stays medial to the apex of the buccal pad.
  • Passes through the pterygotemporal depression.
  • Height: level of the coronoid notch, about 1 cm above the lower occlusal plane. This guide is unreliable when the mouth is wide open.
  • Direction: from the contralateral premolars.
  • Depth: about 25 mm in adults.

Tissues pierced, in order (Dempster)

  1. Mucous membrane, supplied by the faucial isthmus branch of the lingual nerve
  2. Submucosa
  3. Buccinator
  4. Buccopharyngeal fascia (buccinator part)
  5. A fat compartment, possibly the buccal fat pad
  6. Temporopterygoid fascia, after which the needle tip is in the pterygomandibular space
Check: slide 43 skips number (4) and names layer (5) the "pterygopalatine compartment." The pterygopalatine fossa does not lie on this path, which runs through the pterygotemporal region. Confirm this wording with the lecturer.

Lecture 14 · Part 13 · pp. 39–40Complications

Facial nerve palsy after an IAN block

  • Cause: the needle goes too far posterior, into the parotid gland, and the anaesthetic reaches the facial nerve.
  • Effect: temporary facial palsy on the same side. The patient cannot close the eye and the corner of the mouth droops. It lasts as long as the anaesthetic.
Check: the slide calls this "Bell's palsy." Strictly, Bell's palsy means facial palsy with no known cause. This is a temporary palsy caused by the injection.

Eye complication (Kempster 2016)

A patient had hemifacial spasm and eyelid closure on the opposite side after a routine IAN block. Proposed route:

  1. Anaesthetic injected under pressure into the inferior alveolar artery
  2. Reversed flow through the maxillary artery and ECA into the ICA
  3. Ipsilateral MCA
  4. Circle of Willis via the anterior communicating artery
  5. Contralateral ICA/MCA
  6. Contralateral ophthalmic artery
Prevention: aspirate before injecting and inject slowly. (textbook)

Lecture 14 · Part 14 · p. 46IAN Block in Children

  • Success rates are higher because the mandibular foramen is easier to locate.
  • Short needles of 10 mm or 20 mm are enough.
  • The mandibular foramen lies more distal and more inferior relative to the occlusal plane, so the injection goes slightly lower and further back than in adults.
